ai_summary:
Great Britain is generating 12.9 GW of wind power today, with Scottish wind output estimated at 3.4 GW, accounting for 33.7% of installed Scottish wind capacity. Driven by this renewable yield, Scottish carbon intensity sits at 0 gCO2/kWh, contrasting sharply with the GB-wide carbon intensity of 90 gCO2/kWh. Nevertheless, severe transmission bottlenecks between Scotland and major southern demand centres continue to restrict clean energy distribution.

Because network boundaries cannot accommodate this high volume of northern power, Scottish generation curtailed so far today has reached 25.3 GWh through Balancing Mechanism actions, racking up a constraint cost of about £975,156. To compensate for this stranded zero-carbon power, thermal plants elsewhere were forced to ramp up, burning an estimated 4,806,183 m3 of gas and releasing 8,854 tonnes of CO2 into the atmosphere.

Extrapolating this daily constraint spend yields an estimated total yearly cost of £356 million. When recovered across national electricity consumption, this constraint burden adds an estimated £1.20/MWh to UK electricity invoices nationwide, underscoring the direct consumer price penalty and emissions impact resulting from transmission grid limitations.
